title: Why container orchestration
idea: An orchestrator runs containers for you. You declare what should run, and it keeps that true by starting, replacing and spreading containers across machines.
points: By hand, you start, check and replace every container on every machine yourself.
A Docker restart policy revives a crashed container, but only on its own machine.
An orchestrator keeps comparing desired state, what you asked for, with what actually runs.
Amazon ECS is AWS's orchestrator. This chapter runs `bookstore-api` on it.

steps.caption: You declare the desired state: two copies of `bookstore-api`. You do not pick the machines.
The orchestrator starts a copy on each machine. Run by hand, you would visit both machines yourself.
The load balancer spreads requests across both copies.
Machine 2 fails. Run by hand, its container stays gone until you notice.
The balancer sends requests only to the copy that is up, so clients still get answers.
The orchestrator sees one copy against two wanted and starts a replacement on the healthy machine.
You deploy v2 by changing the declared image. The orchestrator replaces copies gradually, keeping the API up.

code.title: Desired vs running
code.caption: A toy model of the check an orchestrator repeats, not ECS code. Predict the output, then set `desired` to 3.

walk.text: Desired state is 2 copies. Two named copies are running now.
Compare: while fewer copies run than wanted, start another one.
Report what is wanted and what runs.
First pass: running matches desired, so nothing changes.
`api-2` crashes. The next pass notices the gap and starts `api-3`.

pitfalls: Skip orchestration for one container on one machine; it adds moving parts to learn.
Store data outside containers: a replacement starts fresh from the image.
Never hard-code one copy's address; a replacement runs somewhere else with a new one.

quiz.q: What does the second line of output show?
quiz.why: The filter removes `api-2`. `reconcile` sees one copy against two wanted and starts `api-3`.

takeaway: Declare the state you want; the orchestrator keeps reality matching it.
